transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The White House is hosting some of the most powerful figures in artificial intelligence
as President Trump pushes back against existential warnings about AI.
The heads of Meta, NVIDIA, Anthropic, Amazon, SpaceX, and OpenAI were among the major tech
leaders who were expected to attend today's lunch divided over whether AI development
needs to be regulated.
However, President Trump is opposed to restrictions on AI development or construction of data
centers.
More voters have protested because of the center's demand on electricity and water
infrastructure.
Aura, the maker of smart health tracking rings, is delaying its plans to go public in what
was expected to be one of this year's blockbuster IPOs, the company citing uncertainty in the
market to push back its listing on the NASDAQ that was set for Wednesday.
Here's NPR's Alina Telliou.
Aura planned to raise up to $2.2 billion in the share sale, which would have valued the
firm at $15 billion.
The company did not say what exactly prompted the delay, claiming there was "strong demand"
for its shares.
In a statement, its CEO says Aura has the luxury of choosing the right moment, and apparently
now is not it.
In fact, Aura is not the first firm to delay its IPO in recent weeks, but it is the highest
profile.
Higher interest rates have been weighing on the markets, and also investors are anxiously
awaiting the IPO of Anthropik, the AI giant.
September is typically a pretty busy time for public listings, but it's been relatively
quiet this year.
Alina Telliou, NPR News.
Lindsay Clancy was back in Massachusetts courtroom today.
Her murder trial ended in a mistrial earlier this month after the jury deadlocked.
Now as NPR's Bill Chappell explains, the judge is weighing what to do next.
Lindsay Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Redington, says she shouldn't be held criminally responsible
for killing her three children back in 2023.
The evidence shows clearly and unequivocally that she was in the state of psychosis.
Prosecutors disagree, saying their evidence shows Clancy had the capacity to know her actions
were wrong.
But the state also declined to set a date for a potential new trial, saying other matters,
like a defense motion to dismiss the case, should be resolved first.
Judge William Sullivan didn't issue any rulings at this hearing, he set the next court date
for November 2nd.
Bill Chappell, NPR News.
Former special counsel Jack Smith is standing by criminal cases he brought against President
Trump.
I stand by my testimony before the House of Representatives, and I will not be silenced
by continued threats of prosecution from the President or others.
Smith testifying at a hearing held by the Senate Judiciary Committee, where Republicans
alleged Smith abused his authority in the course of his investigations.
Smith accused President Trump of breaking the law and trying to overturn the results
of the 2020 election and of mishandling classified documents.
You're listening to NPR News.
The MacArthur Foundation announced the recipients of its prestigious annual fellowship program.
NPR's Chloe Veltman reports, "This year's crop of so-called 'genius' grant winners
are an eclectic bunch."
A historian who studies racial wage gaps, a forensic anthropologist who repatriates
the remains of migrants along the Texas-Mexico border, and a jazz saxophonist whose live performances
include a chef cooking meals on stage.
Their names are Allora DeRenancourt, Kate Spradley, and Emmanuel Wilkins, respectively.
And they are among the 20 recipients of the MacArthur Foundation's No Strings Attached
$800,000 MacArthur Fellowship Grants for 2026.
Wilkins, who recently performed an NPR Tiny Desk concert, likened reinterpreting the music
of jazz greats like John Coltrane to cooking in a recent interview with the arts presenter
SF Jazz.
We're dealing with recipes that you might have gotten from your mother's mother, your
mother's mother's mother.
The MacArthur Fellowship Program is now in its 45th year.
Chloe Veltman, NPR News.
The MacArthur Foundation is a financial supporter of NPR.
Hurricane Polo made landfall in Baja, California as a Category 2 storm this morning.
It brought with it the threat of flash floods and destructive winds of up to 110 miles per
hour.
When the U.S. National Hurricane Center projects, the storm could deliver heavy rain to parts
of the southwestern U.S. later this week.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
That's plus dot NPR dot org.

topics.text: White House hosts AI leaders as Trump opposes regulation of artificial intelligence development
Aura, smart health tracking ring maker, delays planned NASDAQ IPO citing market uncertainty
Lindsay Clancy returns to Massachusetts court as judge considers next steps after mistrial
Former special counsel Jack Smith defends criminal cases against President Trump at Senate hearing
MacArthur Foundation announces 20 recipients of prestigious fellowship grants totaling $800,000 each for 2026
Hurricane Polo makes landfall in Baja California as Category 2 storm with destructive winds
